concepts.title: Probability - A Theoretical Approach
concepts.definition: The theoretical probability of an equally likely event is the ratio of favourable outcomes to the total number of outcomes: a fair coin gives one head out of two outcomes, so the probability of a head is one half - a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
concepts.key_idea: Count fair: favourable outcomes over total equally likely outcomes, always between 0 and 1.

concepts.title: Equally Likely Outcomes and Simple Problems
concepts.definition: The theoretical approach assumes every outcome of the experiment is equally likely - a fair coin, an unbiased die, a well shuffled deck; listing the sample space completely is the first step of every probability problem.
concepts.key_idea: Fair experiment, complete list: the sample space is half the solution.

concepts.title: Complement of an Event
concepts.definition: The complement of an event is its non-happening; since the event and its complement together exhaust all outcomes, their probabilities add to one, so the probability of not E equals one minus the probability of E.
concepts.key_idea: Not E is the rest of the certainty: P(not E) = 1 - P(E).
